meta.title: English Present Tenses Test - Pet Theme
meta.description: A comprehensive test covering English Present Tenses.
meta.info: This test includes 30 questions focusing on combined grammar structures involving Simple Present, Present Continuous, Present Perfect, and Present Perfect Continuous tenses, paired with topics like gerunds, relative clauses, passive voice, quantifiers, and more, all within familiar pet contexts.
meta.author: Qwen3.7

data.hint: Choose the correct verb forms to complete the sentence.
data.question: My golden retriever usually _____ his favorite toys under the sofa, but today he _____ them in the kitchen.

explanation.text: This combines the Simple Present tense for habitual actions ('usually hides') with the Present Continuous tense for actions happening around the present moment ('is leaving').
explanation.concept: Contrasting habitual actions with current temporary actions
explanation.formula: Subject + usually + base verb + s/es, but today + subject + am/is/are + verb-ing
examples: She usually drinks coffee, but today she is drinking tea.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Continuous tense with subject-verb agreement. 'Cats' is plural, requiring 'are'. 'Dog' is singular, requiring 'is barking'.
explanation.concept: Correct auxiliary verbs for plural and singular subjects in continuous tenses
explanation.formula: Plural subject + are + verb-ing; singular subject + is + verb-ing
examples: The birds are singing, while the cat is sleeping.

data.hint: Choose the correct prepositions to complete the sentence.
data.question: I have been looking _____ my lost hamster _____ three hours, but I haven't found him yet.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Perfect Continuous tense with preposition collocations. 'Looking' is followed by 'for' when searching, and 'for' is used with a duration of time ('three hours').
explanation.concept: Correct preposition usage with phrasal verbs and time expressions
explanation.formula: Have/has been looking for + noun + for + period of time
examples: I have been waiting for the bus for twenty minutes.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Perfect Continuous and Present Perfect Passive tenses with quantifiers. 'Many of the puppies' is plural, requiring 'have been'. 'Much of the mud' is uncountable and singular, requiring 'has been'.
explanation.concept: Agreement with plural and uncountable quantifiers in perfect tenses
explanation.formula: Many of + plural noun + have been + verb-ing; much of + uncountable noun + has been + past participle
examples: Many of the items have been sold, but much of the stock has been kept.

data.hint: Choose the correct verb forms to complete the sentence.
data.question: My parrot enjoys _____ seeds, but it refuses _____ vegetables.

explanation.text: This combines the Simple Present tense with gerund and infinitive verb patterns. 'Enjoy' is always followed by a gerund ('eating'), while 'refuse' is followed by a to-infinitive ('to eat').
explanation.concept: Specific verbs requiring gerund or infinitive complements
explanation.formula: Subject + enjoys + verb-ing, but + subject + refuses + to-infinitive
examples: She enjoys reading, but she refuses to study math.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Continuous tense with non-defining relative clauses and Simple Present subject-verb agreement. 'Vet' is singular, requiring 'who is' and 'says'. 'It' is singular, requiring 'needs'.
explanation.topic: Present Continuous + Relative Clauses + Subject-Verb Agreement
explanation.concept: Singular agreement in relative clauses and main clauses
explanation.formula: Singular noun, who + is + verb-ing, + says + that + it + needs
examples: The doctor, who is treating the patient, says that he needs rest.

data.hint: Choose the correct verb forms to complete the sentence.
data.question: The new aquarium _____ already _____ by the marine biologist, so the fish can move in tomorrow.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Perfect tense with the passive voice. The singular subject 'aquarium' requires 'has', and the passive structure requires 'been' + past participle ('set up').
explanation.concept: Completed actions in the present perfect passive
explanation.formula: Singular subject + has + been + past participle
examples: The room has already been cleaned.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Continuous (as a state) with advanced comparatives and Simple Present subject-verb agreement. 'Smarter' is already comparative, so 'more' is redundant. 'She' requires the singular verb 'eats'.
explanation.concept: Correct comparative forms and third-person singular agreement
explanation.formula: Subject + is + comparative adjective; singular subject + always + verb + s/es
examples: He is faster than me, and he always runs ahead.

data.hint: Choose the correct verb forms to complete the sentence.
data.question: Since we adopted the rescue dog, he _____ constantly _____ at the mail carrier.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Perfect Continuous tense with time clauses. 'Since' triggers the perfect aspect, and 'constantly' with 'has been barking' emphasizes the ongoing, repeated nature of the action up to the present.
explanation.concept: Ongoing actions starting in the past and continuing to the present
explanation.formula: Since + past event, subject + has/have + been + verb-ing
examples: Since it started raining, we have constantly been waiting inside.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Continuous tense with phrasal verbs and gerund patterns. 'Without' is a preposition and must be followed by a gerund ('making'), not a to-infinitive.
explanation.concept: Gerunds required after prepositions
explanation.formula: Subject + am/is/are + verb-ing + without + verb-ing
examples: He is running without making a sound.

data.hint: Choose the correct verb forms to complete the sentence.
data.question: A responsible pet owner always _____ fresh water available, and they _____ neglect their animal's needs.

explanation.text: This combines the Simple Present tense with adverbs of frequency and modal verbs. 'Owner' is singular, requiring 'keeps'. 'Must not' expresses a strong prohibition or obligation.
explanation.concept: Third-person singular agreement and modal expressions of obligation
explanation.formula: Singular subject + always + verb + s/es; subject + must not + base verb
examples: A good driver always checks the mirrors, and they must not use a phone.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Perfect tense with adverbial clauses of concession. The singular subject 'turtle' requires the singular auxiliary 'has', not 'have'.
explanation.concept: Subject-verb agreement in concessive clauses
explanation.formula: Although + singular subject + has + past participle
examples: Although the cat has lived here for years, it is still shy.

data.hint: Choose the correct discourse marker to complete the sentence.
data.question: The bird is molting its feathers; _____, it requires extra protein in its diet right now.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Continuous tense with discourse markers. 'Therefore' is used to show a logical result or consequence of the ongoing action (molting requires extra protein).
explanation.concept: Using resultative discourse markers with present continuous contexts
explanation.formula: Subject + is/are + verb-ing; therefore, + subject + requires
examples: It is raining heavily; therefore, we are staying indoors.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Perfect Continuous tense with article usage. 'Unique' starts with a consonant sound (/j/), so it correctly takes the indefinite article 'a', not 'an'.
explanation.concept: Indefinite articles before words starting with a /j/ sound
explanation.formula: Have/has been + verb-ing + a + word starting with /j/ sound
examples: She has been building a unique portfolio.

data.hint: Choose the correct verb form to complete the elliptical sentence.
data.question: My sister feeds the fish every morning, and I _____ every evening.

explanation.text: This combines the Simple Present tense with ellipsis. The auxiliary 'do' is used to avoid repeating the full verb phrase ('feed the fish').
explanation.concept: Omitting repeated verb phrases using auxiliary verbs
explanation.formula: Subject + base verb + s/es + object, and + subject + do/does
examples: He washes the car on Saturdays, and I do on Sundays.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Perfect tense with verb patterns. 'Decide' is followed by a to-infinitive ('to adopt'), and 'avoid' is followed by a gerund ('telling').
explanation.concept: Specific verbs requiring infinitive or gerund complements
explanation.formula: Have/has decided + to-infinitive; have/has avoided + verb-ing
examples: We have decided to move, and we have avoided telling anyone.

data.hint: Choose the correct verb forms to complete the sentence.
data.question: We _____ the new puppy to the vet tomorrow afternoon, so we _____ a carrier right now.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Continuous tense for future arrangements with the Present Continuous for actions happening right now.
explanation.concept: Using Present Continuous for fixed future plans and current actions
explanation.formula: Subject + am/is/are + verb-ing (future) + , so + subject + am/is/are + verb-ing (now)
examples: We are meeting tomorrow, so we are preparing today.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines the Simple Present tense with subject-verb agreement for collective nouns and quantifiers. 'Flock' is a singular collective noun, requiring 'flies'. 'A number of' means 'several' and takes a plural verb ('stay').
explanation.concept: Agreement with collective nouns and 'a number of'
explanation.formula: Singular collective noun + verb + s/es; a number of + plural noun + base verb
examples: The team plays well, but a number of fans complain.

data.hint: Choose the correct verb form to complete the sentence.
data.question: The leash, which I _____ for years, has finally snapped.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Perfect tense with non-defining relative clauses. 'Have used' indicates an action that started in the past and continues up to the present moment of snapping.
explanation.concept: Present Perfect in relative clauses describing duration up to the present
explanation.formula: Noun, which + subject + have/has + past participle, + present perfect/present simple
examples: The car, which I have owned for years, finally broke down.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Perfect Continuous and Present Continuous tenses with preposition collocations. 'Relying' is followed by 'on', and 'accustomed' is followed by 'to'.
explanation.concept: Correct preposition usage after specific verbs and adjectives
explanation.formula: Has been relying on + noun; is accustomed to + verb-ing
examples: He has been relying on his friend, and he is accustomed to helping others.

data.hint: Choose the correct verb forms to complete the sentence.
data.question: If a dog _____ its tail rapidly, it usually _____ happy or excited.

explanation.text: This combines the Simple Present tense in a Zero Conditional structure. Both the 'if' clause and the main clause use the Simple Present to express a general truth or scientific fact.
explanation.concept: Expressing general truths with 'if' + present simple
explanation.formula: If + singular subject + verb + s/es, subject + is/are + adjective
examples: If water reaches 100°C, it boils.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Continuous passive voice with subject-verb agreement. 'Feed' must be the past participle 'fed'. 'Tanks' is plural, requiring 'are being'.
explanation.concept: Correct past participle forms and plural agreement in passive voice
explanation.formula: Plural subject + are being + past participle
examples: The rooms are being cleaned right now.

data.hint: Choose the correct quantifiers to complete the sentence.
data.question: _____ of the rescued kittens have found homes, but _____ of the stray population remains unadopted.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Perfect and Simple Present tenses with quantifiers. 'Kittens' is a countable plural noun, requiring 'Many'. 'Population' is treated as an uncountable/singular concept here, requiring 'much'.
explanation.concept: Countable vs. uncountable quantifiers
explanation.formula: Many of + plural countable noun + have + past participle; much of + uncountable noun + remains
examples: Many of the books have sold, but much of the work remains.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines the Simple Present tense with adverbs of frequency and subject-verb agreement. 'She' requires the singular verb 'prefers'. (Note: 'Rarely the cat sleeps' is acceptable in some poetic contexts, but standard inversion 'Rarely does the cat sleep' is preferred. However, 'prefer' is definitively an error).
explanation.concept: Third-person singular agreement with adverbs of frequency
explanation.formula: Singular subject + always + verb + s/es
examples: He always prefers tea over coffee.

data.hint: Choose the correct conjunction to complete the sentence.
data.question: The horse has been galloping in the pasture all morning, _____ it looks exhausted now.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Perfect Continuous tense with conjunctions of result. 'So' correctly links the ongoing past-to-present action (galloping) with its present result (looks exhausted).
explanation.concept: Using resultative conjunctions with perfect continuous contexts
explanation.formula: Subject + has/have been + verb-ing + all + time, so + subject + present simple
examples: It has been raining all day, so the ground is wet.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Continuous tense with gerund verb patterns. Both 'considering' and 'dreading' must be followed by a gerund ('getting', 'handling'), not a to-infinitive.
explanation.concept: Verbs requiring gerund complements in continuous tenses
explanation.formula: Am/is/are + considering/dreading + verb-ing
examples: I am considering moving, but I am dreading packing.

data.hint: Choose the correct verb forms to complete the cleft sentence.
data.question: It _____ the veterinarian who _____ the most accurate diagnosis for my pet.

explanation.text: This combines the Simple Present tense with cleft sentences for emphasis. 'It is' emphasizes the subject, and the relative pronoun 'who' refers to the singular 'veterinarian', requiring 'makes'.
explanation.concept: Subject-verb agreement in it-cleft structures
explanation.formula: It + is + singular noun + who/that + verb + s/es
examples: It is the teacher who explains the concept clearly.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines the Simple Present with modal verbs of deduction in the perfect form. Modal verbs ('must', 'can't') are always followed by the base form 'have', never 'has'.
explanation.topic: Simple Present + Modal Verbs of Deduction
explanation.concept: Base form of 'have' after modal verbs
explanation.formula: Subject + must/can't + have + past participle
examples: He must have forgotten his keys.

data.hint: Choose the correct verb forms to complete the sentence.
data.question: As the puppy grows, it _____ more energetic, and its tricks _____ increasingly complex.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Continuous tense with conjunctions of time to describe changing situations. 'Is becoming' and 'are becoming' emphasize ongoing development.
explanation.concept: Describing changing situations and trends with 'as'
explanation.formula: As + subject + verb + s/es, subject + is/are + becoming + adjective
examples: As the weather is getting colder, the days are becoming shorter.

data.hint: Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This combines the Present Perfect passive voice with time clauses. The past participles 'washed' and 'trimmed' are required after 'has/have been'.
explanation.topic: Present Perfect + Passive Voice + Time Clauses
explanation.concept: Correct past participle forms in Present Perfect passive
explanation.formula: By the time + present simple, subject + has/have been + past participle
examples: By the time we arrive, the food will have been eaten.
